Vulnerability Title: The unauthenticated verify-user endpoint is an account existence oracle callable for any email or mobile
Description: verifyUser at src/services/auth.ts:17-28 posts to /verify-user with a caller supplied type of email or mobile and a value - and the endpoint requires no authentication. checkEmailExists and checkPhoneExists at src/helpers/auth.ts:396-478 call it from the registration form and the complete-profile modal on every field blur so the request shape is trivially observable and repeatable. The response distinguishes a registered identifier from an unregistered one: a hit returns success true and the caller marks the field as taken at :412 and :455 while a miss surfaces as an error the service converts into a success false fallback. Nothing in the client rate limits or debounces the probe beyond the field blur. Combined with code review issue 13 the probed value also travels in the URL query string so every probe is recorded in access and proxy logs.
Attack Vector: Any unauthenticated visitor - no account or token required
Preconditions: None - the endpoint is reachable without authentication.
Steps to Reproduce / PoC: 1. POST /api/verify-user with type email and a known registered address and read the response. 2. Repeat with an address that is not registered. 3. Compare the two responses - they differ deterministically. 4. Script the request across a list of addresses or mobile numbers.
Expected (Secure) Behavior: Existence checks are rate limited and return a uniform response so a registered identifier cannot be distinguished from an unregistered one by an unauthenticated caller.
Actual Behavior: The two cases are distinguishable and the probe can be repeated without limit.
Impact: An attacker can confirm which email addresses and mobile numbers hold accounts on the platform - which turns a generic credential-stuffing or phishing list into a targeted one and leaks customer membership. Mobile enumeration is the more sensitive half because the number is also the OTP delivery channel.
Remediation: Rate limit /verify-user per IP and per identifier on the panel and return a uniform response regardless of existence - moving the real check into the registration submission where it is already enforced. If the inline availability hint is worth keeping require a CAPTCHA or a signed token for it. Panel change - coordinate rather than changing the contract unilaterally.

Vulnerability Title: The OTP resend control has no cooldown so codes can be requested as fast as the requests complete
Description: The resend buttons in both OTP flows are gated only by the in-flight loading flag - src/features/auth/components/LoginForm.tsx:214-221 binds isLoading to otp.isResending and ForgotPasswordForm.tsx:149-156 does the same with forgot.isResending. Neither carries a countdown - a disabled window - or an attempt counter so the control re-enables the instant the previous request resolves and can be pressed again immediately. The handlers behind them do not throttle either: handleResendOtp at src/helpers/auth.ts:332-393 clears and re-initialises the reCAPTCHA verifier and sends again with no timing check - and the custom gateway path calls sendForgotOtp at src/features/auth/useForgotPassword.ts:97 with no guard. For the Firebase phone path Firebase applies its own quotas but the custom SMS gateway path is limited only by whatever the panel enforces.
CWE: CWE-770 Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
Attack Vector: Any visitor who can reach the OTP step - which needs only a phone number or an account identifier
Preconditions: The OTP step of either the login or the forgot-password flow.
Steps to Reproduce / PoC: 1. Enter an identifier and reach the OTP step. 2. Press resend and wait for the request to resolve. 3. Press resend again immediately and repeat - observe there is no cooldown and no attempt cap.
Expected (Secure) Behavior: A resend cooldown of some tens of seconds and a cap on resends per identifier per window - enforced on the client for usability and on the panel for security.
Actual Behavior: The control re-enables immediately and resends without limit.
Impact: SMS cost abuse against the platform's gateway and SMS flooding of a chosen number - both driven from an unauthenticated flow. Repeated resends also invalidate and reissue codes which can be used to grief a legitimate customer mid-login.
Remediation: Add a countdown to both resend controls that disables the button for a fixed window and caps resends per identifier - and confirm the panel throttles the send endpoints independently since a client cooldown is a usability control and not a security boundary.

Vulnerability Title: The offline cart survives logout and is merged into the next account that signs in on the device
Description: The offlineCart slice is persisted - it is in the redux-persist whitelist at src/lib/redux/store.ts:15 - so it is written to localStorage and survives a browser restart. clearOfflineCart is dispatched from exactly one place: syncOfflineCartToServer at src/helpers/updators.ts:110 and only on the success branch. handleLogout at src/helpers/auth.ts:656-684 clears the auth and cart and recentlyViewed slices and never clears offlineCart. So whenever the slice is non-empty at sign out it stays on the device - which is the normal outcome when a guest added items and never signed in - and also when a previous sync failed since the failure branch at :135-149 returns without clearing. Every login path then calls syncOfflineCartToServer before anything else - google at src/helpers/auth.ts:120 - apple at :225 - password at :608 and phone OTP at :771 - so the leftover items are posted into the NEW account server cart the moment the next person signs in on that device.
CWE: CWE-1188 Insecure Default Initialization of Resource
Attack Vector: Local access to a shared device - a family or office or public machine where one person signs out and another signs in
Preconditions: A non-empty offline cart at sign out - a guest session that added items or a sync that previously failed.
Steps to Reproduce / PoC: 1. As a guest add items to the cart on a shared device so the offline cart is populated. 2. Sign in as user A and then sign out - or leave the guest session and let a second person use the browser. 3. Sign in as user B on the same device. 4. Read user B server cart.
Expected (Secure) Behavior: The offline cart is scoped to the browsing session that created it and is discarded at sign out so it can never cross accounts.
Actual Behavior: The leftover items are silently merged into whichever account signs in next.
Impact: User B account receives products user A chose which discloses what A was shopping for and can be bought by accident at checkout. It also corrupts B cart totals without any action by B. The merge is silent - there is no prompt and no notice.
Remediation: Dispatch clearOfflineCart from handleLogout alongside the existing slice clears - and clear it on the sync failure branch too so a failed sync cannot leave items behind for the next account. If carrying a guest cart across a sign in is deliberate then prompt before merging rather than merging silently.

Vulnerability Title: Razorpay and Paystack declare payment success from a bare client callback and discard the reference the gateway hands them
Description: Two of the four gateways treat the SDK success callback as proof of payment and forward nothing to the panel for verification. Razorpay registers handler: async () => at src/components/PaymentGateway/RazorPay.tsx:205 for the order flow and :149 for the wallet flow - the callback takes no argument so razorpay_payment_id and razorpay_signature which Razorpay passes to that handler are discarded rather than posted for checking. Paystack does the same at src/components/PaymentGateway/Paystack.tsx:140 with onSuccess: () => confirmSuccess() - and the reference and trxref fields it would receive are declared in the response type at :8 and :13 yet never read. Stripe in the same codebase demonstrates the correct shape: it calls stripe.confirmPayment at Stripe.tsx:77-85 and inspects the returned error and paymentIntent at :98-106 before treating the payment as done - so the success signal comes from the gateway API rather than from a fire-and-forget callback. WHAT IS VERIFIED HERE - the two callbacks discard the payment reference and no verification request is issued from the client. WHAT IS NOT VERIFIABLE FROM THIS REPOSITORY - whether the panel verifies the gateway webhook signature server side which is the control that actually settles payment state. The finding is the storefront total dependence on that unconfirmed control plus the loss of the reference that would let it cross-check.
CWE: CWE-345 Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity
Attack Vector: Anyone able to invoke the page callback in their own browser - the practical risk is a customer marking their own order paid in the UI rather than a third party stealing funds
Preconditions: A checkout reaching the Razorpay or Paystack step.
Steps to Reproduce / PoC: 1. Begin a payment through Razorpay or Paystack. 2. Invoke the registered success handler from the console without completing payment. 3. Observe the client proceeds to its success path having sent no reference to the panel.
Expected (Secure) Behavior: The gateway reference is forwarded to the panel and the success state is shown only once the panel confirms the payment - as the Stripe path effectively does by checking the returned paymentIntent.
Actual Behavior: The client declares success from a callback that carries no proof and discards the identifiers that would allow verification.
Impact: If panel webhook verification is missing or delayed the customer sees a paid state the backend has not recorded - and support cannot reconcile because the reference was never captured on this side. It also removes the storefront ability to detect a mismatch between what the gateway says and what the panel recorded.
Remediation: Capture the payment reference in both handlers and post it to a panel verification endpoint - showing success only on its response - matching the shape the Stripe integration already uses. Separately confirm with the panel team that webhook signatures are verified over the raw body and that events are deduplicated - and record that answer here so the dependency stops being an assumption.
